Why Valuable

“YOU will have to know that I am Jehovah.” (36:11) Jehovah inspired Ezekiel to express this thought more than 60 times in the book bearing his name. And the phrase “Sovereign Lord Jehovah” appears over 200 times. Jehovah uses this book​—more than any other—​to emphasize the importance of his name, or reputation. He also reveals his purpose to clear his name of reproach. (36:22; 39:7) When Jehovah sanctifies his name, his faithful worshippers will benefit greatly.​—34:25-28; 39:25.

2 What does Jehovah mean when he says: “You will have to know that I am Jehovah”? This phrase means that people will have no choice but to recognize his sovereignty and what his name means. The disobedient Jews in Ezekiel’s day came to know one aspect of Jehovah’s personality when they experienced his discipline. (6:9, 10) In the future, the nations “will have to know” Jehovah as Judge when he executes vengeance on them. (25:17) However, true worshippers will also come to know Jehovah as the Fulfiller of promises when he rewards them with eternal peace and happiness.​—28:26.

3 The book of Ezekiel contains details about the promised Messiah, who would be a descendant of King David. For example, although David’s throne would sit empty for a long time, Jehovah swore that the Kingdom would eventually be given to the one with the legal right, the Messiah. (21:27) Jehovah also said that he would “raise up one shepherd . . . , my servant David.” (34:23, 24) Jesus, a descendant of David, fulfilled these prophecies. (Lu 1:32, 33; Joh 10:11) The book of Ezekiel includes many other prophecies that strengthen our faith.​—See Box 26-A.

Summary

12 Jehovah commissions Ezekiel as a prophet. (1:1–3:27) In 613 B.C.E., the heavens are opened and Ezekiel begins “to see visions of God.” (1:1) Ezekiel sees impressive living creatures, later identified as cherubs. (10:20) He sees a celestial chariot and a brilliant light like “the appearance of the glory of Jehovah.” (1:28) Jehovah then commissions Ezekiel as a watchman and as a prophet. (2:3) Whether others listen or not, Ezekiel must faithfully warn them; otherwise, he will die.​—3:17-19.

13 Ezekiel prophesies judgment against Jerusalem and its rebellious people. (4:1–24:27) Jehovah commands Ezekiel to act out the coming siege of Jerusalem and the famine its inhabitants will experience. (4:1-3, 10) He tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard and instructs him on what to do with the hair. These actions portray the thorough destruction of Jerusalem and its people. (5:1, 2) Then he tells the prophet to denounce the Israelites for their idolatry.​—6:1-4.

14 In 612 B.C.E., Ezekiel is taken to Jerusalem in a vision and sees the detestable worship taking place there. (8:1-3) A man goes through the city, putting a mark on those sighing and groaning over what is taking place. Executioners then kill off everyone without the mark. (9:1-6) Yes, Jehovah will punish the nation. (11:9, 10) However, some exiles will return to Jerusalem.​—11:17.

15 Jehovah has Ezekiel act out the exile of the Jews. (12:3-7) Then He commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Israel’s false prophets. (13:2) The Jewish elders in Babylon speak with Ezekiel, and he informs them that nothing can stop Jerusalem’s destruction from happening.​—14:1, 14.

16 Jehovah uses vivid illustrations to explain the reason for Jerusalem’s destruction. He compares Jerusalem to the wood of a vine that is fit only for burning and likens her to a beloved wife who becomes a brazen prostitute. (15:6; 16:3, 8, 28) In a riddle, he compares King Zedekiah to a vine that will dry up. (17:7, 9, 12) Yet, Jehovah assures Israel that each person will be judged for his own actions and that the righteous will keep living. (18:20-22) Ezekiel is then told to sing a dirge, or a song of mourning, about Israel’s rulers.​—19:1, ftn.
